title: The Hebrew Feature Against Its Closest Neuron
takeaway: The neuron whose activations track the Hebrew feature most closely does not behave like the feature: the correlation is 0.1 on activations and 0.38 on logit weights, and in both plots the feature's axis cleanly separates Hebrew while the neuron's axis does not. The paper takes this as evidence that dictionary learning did not simply hand back an already-Hebrew neuron under a new name.
walkthrough:
Two scatter plots, side by side. Both compare one learned feature against one neuron of the transformer's MLP. The feature is A/1/416, the [[hebrew-feature]]; in the paper's [[feature-notation]] that reads transformer A, dictionary learning run 1, feature number 416. The neuron is A/neurons/489, one of the MLP's 512 neurons.

That neuron was not picked at random. It is the [[most-correlated-neuron]] — the one whose activations track this feature's most closely over roughly 40 million dataset examples. If any single neuron were quietly doing this feature's job, it would be this one.

In both panels the feature is on the vertical axis and the neuron on the horizontal. Dots are colored by the [[hebrew-script-proxy]], a log-likelihood ratio for Hebrew text: red is Hebrew, blue is not.

### Left panel: activations

One dot per dataset token. Its height is the feature's activation there. Its horizontal position is neuron 489's activation on that same token. Both axes run 0 to 9, with a break separating exactly zero from the ">0" range, because most of the mass sits at zero.

The red cloud sits high, roughly 6.5 to 8.2 on the feature axis. Horizontally it spreads across about 1.5 to 3.5, mixed in with blue points at those same neuron values. The printed [[pearson-correlation]] is 0.1.

Now read the marginal strips along each edge. The strip beside the y-axis turns red toward the top. The strip under the x-axis stays blue across the whole neuron range, carrying only a thin red trace. Knowing the feature is high tells you the token is Hebrew; knowing the neuron is high does not.

### Right panel: logit weights

Here one dot is one vocabulary token. Its height is the feature's [[logit-weight]] on that token — how much the feature firing pushes that token's next-token logit up or down. Its horizontal position is the neuron's weight on the same token. Both axes run $-0.6$ to $0.6$.

A dense blue cloud sits at the origin, tilted slightly upward, ringed and labelled "Interference Weights?". That is the paper's guess that the shared near-zero mass is [[weight-interference]] forced by [[superposition]] rather than deliberate behavior; the question mark is the authors' own. The printed correlation, 0.38, comes largely from that cloud.

The red ellipse at the upper right holds the Hebrew tokens, sitting near 0.42 to 0.55 on the feature axis. The feature axis separates them from everything else. Their neuron weights, roughly 0.1 to 0.35, sit inside the blue cloud's own horizontal spread.

Both panels make the same point in the same way, which is the check the paper calls [[feature-neuron-nonalignment]].

terms.definition: Marks the left plot as comparing per-token activation values — how strongly the feature and the neuron each fire on the same piece of text. Each point is one token from the dataset.
Marks the right plot as comparing weights onto output logits rather than activations. Each point is one element of the model's vocabulary.
The Hebrew feature: transformer A, dictionary learning run 1, feature index 416. It is a learned direction in MLP activation space, not a neuron.
Neuron 489 of transformer A's 512-unit MLP. The 'neurons' slot in the notation marks this as an actual neuron of the transformer rather than an autoencoder feature.
The subtitle of each panel, giving the Pearson correlation between the quantity plotted on the y-axis (the feature) and the one on the x-axis (the neuron). 'A' here is the feature A/1/416.
The activation of feature A/1/416 on a given dataset token, as read off the sparse autoencoder's hidden layer. (The label carries a typo in the original.)
The post-ReLU activation of neuron 489 on that same dataset token.

For one vocabulary token, how much that token's next-token logit moves when feature A/1/416 is active, computed by pushing the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding.

terms.term: Logit Weight (Run A Neuron) — right x-axis
terms.definition: The same quantity computed for neuron 489 instead of the feature: how much that neuron's activity moves each token's logit.
The Hebrew script proxy score for the token, a log-likelihood ratio built from Unicode blocks. Red means the token scores as Hebrew, blue means it does not.

The narrow colored bands along the left edge and the bottom edge of each plot. Each collapses the scatter onto one axis, showing what fraction of points at each value along that axis is Hebrew (red) versus not (blue).

A break in both activation axes separating the spike of tokens at exactly zero from the continuous range above zero. Without the break, the zero atom would swamp the plot, since most tokens do not fire the feature or the neuron at all.

The labelled red ellipse in the right panel, marking the vocabulary tokens the Hebrew proxy scores as Hebrew — including the \xd7 byte that begins the UTF-8 encoding of most basic-block Hebrew characters.

The labelled blue ellipse around the central mass of near-zero logit weights. The paper's suggestion, with the question mark as printed, is that this mass is unwanted cross-talk forced by superposition rather than behavior the model intends.
Hand-drawn guides around the two clusters in the right panel, not fitted confidence regions. They are there to point the eye at the second mode and at the central cloud.

terms.term: Dashed crosshair at the origin (right panel)
terms.definition: Reference lines at zero logit weight on both axes. Zero is meaningful because logit weights are shifted so that each feature's median weight is zero; the softmax is shift-invariant, so only relative weights matter.

The selection rule that put neuron 489 in these plots: over roughly 40 million dataset examples, its activations correlate with this feature's more than any other neuron's do. It is the paper's preferred search for a neuron counterpart to a feature.

numbers.meaning: Pearson correlation between the feature's activations and neuron 489's activations, printed above the left panel. It is the highest such value over all 512 neurons, which is why the paper says there is no similar neuron.

Pearson correlation between the feature's logit weights and the neuron's logit weights, printed above the right panel. It is higher than the activation correlation, but the plot shows the agreement concentrated in the central near-zero cloud the paper tentatively calls interference, not in the Hebrew tokens.
The feature's index within dictionary learning run A/1. It carries no meaning beyond identifying the feature.
The dictionary learning run in the feature's name. Runs differ in dictionary size and in the L1 coefficient used.
The index of the neuron in the transformer's MLP. This is the same neuron that turned out to be most correlated with the Arabic script feature, which the paper reads as a multi-language neuron.
The number of neurons in the one-layer transformer's MLP, so the size of the pool searched for a neuron counterpart to the feature.
The residual stream width of the transformer being studied. Not printed on the figure, but it is the dimension the 512 MLP neurons write back into.
The number of dataset examples over which activation correlations were computed to pick the most correlated neuron. A large sample matters because Hebrew text is rare in the corpus.
The range of both axes in the left panel. It is set by the feature, whose activations reach about 9; the neuron's activations stop near 4.5 to 5, leaving the right half of the panel empty.
The vertical band where the red (Hebrew) points sit in the left panel — the feature's strong-activation regime, which the paper says is where its specificity to Hebrew is high.
The horizontal spread of those same red points, i.e. what neuron 489 was doing on Hebrew tokens. Blue non-Hebrew points occupy the same range, which is why the neuron's axis fails to separate Hebrew.
The range of both axes in the right panel, covering the logit weight distribution for both the feature and the neuron after the median-zero shift.
Where the Hebrew token cluster sits on the feature's logit weight axis. This matches the small second mode on the far right of the feature's own logit weight histogram.
Where those same Hebrew tokens sit on the neuron's logit weight axis. The range lies inside the bulk blue cloud, so the neuron's weights give no separated Hebrew mode.

The bulk of the blue cloud in the right panel on both axes. Nearly all vocabulary tokens get a small weight from both the feature and the neuron, which is what the 'Interference Weights?' label is pointing at.
The scale of the Hebrew log-likelihood ratio driving the red/blue coloring, as printed on the companion activation and logit histograms for this feature. Positive is Hebrew-leaning, negative is not.

Context from the surrounding section, not printed here: the Pearson correlation between the Hebrew script proxy and the feature's activations. It is the yardstick against which the neuron's 0.1 should be read.

The corresponding activation and logit weight correlations in the matching figure for the Arabic script feature, which uses the same neuron 489. The Hebrew numbers are slightly higher but the paper reads both cases the same way.
